## Claims

### C1 — OT as “bone and marrow” of Hebrews
**Claim (Cockerill):** The OT is the “bone and marrow” of Hebrews; from beginning to end the book is an expository “sermon” resting on careful OT interpretation.  
**Quote:** “The OT is the \"bone and marrow\" of Hebrews. From beginning to end this book is an expository \"sermon\" that rests on careful OT interpretation.”  
**Locus:** L1477

### C2 — Twenty-eight OT quotations catalogued (canonical order)
**Claim (Cockerill):** The pastor quotes twenty-eight OT passages (listed in canonical order), using “quotation” only where there is an introductory formula and close wording of the OT text.  
**Quote:** “He quotes the following twenty-eight OT passages, listed here in canonical order: Gen 2:2 (Heb 4:4); 21:12 (Heb 11:18); 22:16-17 (Heb 6:14); Exod 24:8 (Heb 9:20); 25:40 (Heb 8:5); Deut 9:19 (Heb 12:21); 31:6 (Heb 13:5); 32:35 (Heb 10:30a); 32:36 (Heb 10:30b); 32:43 (Heb 6:1); 2 Sam 7:14 (Heb 1:5a); Ps 2:7 (Heb 1:5b; 5:5); 8:4-6 (Heb 2:5-10); 22:22 (Heb 2:12); 40:6-8 (Heb 10:5-10); 45:6-7 (Heb 1:8-9); 95:7-11 (Heb 3:7-11); 102:25-27 (Heb 1:10-12); 104:4 (Heb 1:7); 110:1 (Heb 1:13); 110:4 (Heb 5:6; 7:17, 21); Ps 118:6 (Heb 13:6); Prov 3:11-12 (Heb 12:5-6); Isa 8:17 (Heb 2:13a); Isa 8:18 (Heb 2:13b); Jer 31:31-34 (Heb 8:7-13; 10:15-18); Hab 2:3-4 (Heb 10:37-38); Hag 2:6 (Heb 12:26).”  
**Locus:** L1477  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]]

### C3 — Thirty-two quotation instances; only Hebrew-OT canon quoted
**Claim (Cockerill):** Twenty-five of the twenty-eight passages are quoted once; Ps 2:7 and Jer 31:31–34 twice; Ps 110:4 three times — thirty-two OT quotations total. Hebrews may allude to or echo other literature but quotes only from the canonical books of the Hebrew OT (NT pattern).  
**Quote:** “The pastor quotes twenty-five of these passages once, two of them (Ps 2:7; Jer 31:31-34) twice, and one (Ps 110:4) three times, making a total of thirty-two OT quotations. … In accord with the NT pattern, Hebrews may allude to or echo other literature but quotes only from the canonical books of the Hebrew OT.”  
**Locus:** L1477

### C4 — Fundamental hermeneutical principles from Heb 1:1–4
**Claim (Cockerill):** Heb 1:1–4 states the principles underlying the pastor’s OT interpretation: (1) the God who “spoke” through the OT has now “spoken” in one who is Son — continuous with and the fulfillment of all said before the Son assumed humanity; (2) continuity of human recipients — those addressed through the prophets are the “fathers” of those addressed in the Son; one God and one people of God.  
**Quote:** “Heb 1:1-4 enunciates the fundamental principles that underlie his interpretation of the OT. First, the God who \"spoke\" through the OT has now \"spoken\" in one who is Son. … this final word in the Son is both continuous with, and the fulfillment of, all that God said before the Son assumed humanity. Second, … Those to whom God spoke through the prophets were the \"fathers\" of those he addresses in his Son (1:1-2). … There is one God and one people of God.”  
**Locus:** L1481  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[new-covenant]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]]

### C5 — One people on pilgrimage to the same heavenly city
**Claim (Cockerill):** Both those before and after Christ received the same call, promise, and “gospel,” and are on pilgrimage to the same heavenly “city,” which all the faithful obtain through Christ.  
**Quote:** “Both those who live before and after Christ have received the same call, the same promise, the same \"gospel,\" and are on pilgrimage to the same heavenly \"city,\" which all the faithful will obtain through Christ.”  
**Locus:** L1481  
**Suggested pages:** [[promised-land]], [[hebrews]]

### C6 — Immediacy of God’s word; prefer direct-address OT speech
**Claim (Cockerill):** Continuity of divine speaker and human addressees underlies the immediacy of God’s word; the pastor prefers OT passages in the form of direct address and introduces them with verbs of speech rather than “it is written.” God “speaks” in the present by past words to the people of old and by conversations with the Son concerning incarnation and exaltation.  
**Quote:** “This firm confidence in the continuity of the divine speaker and of the human addressees underlies the pastor's sense of the immediacy of God's word. Thus it is no surprise that he prefers OT passages that are in the form of direct address and that he introduces them with verbs denoting speech rather than with \"it is What God has said in the past is of more than anti quarian interest. God \"speaks\" to his people in the present both by the words that he spoke to his people of old (Heb 3:7-4:11; 10:36-39) and by his conversations with his Son concerning the Son's incarnation and exaltation (1:114; 2:11-13; 7:1-28; 10:5-10).”  
**Locus:** L1483

### C7 — Final revelation is the fully adequate Savior, not only Son’s words
**Claim (Cockerill):** God’s final revelation embraces more than what the Son has said; it is found in the fully adequate Savior he has become through incarnation, obedience, self-offering, and session.  
**Quote:** “God's final revelation embraces more than what the Son has said. God's final revelation is found in the fully adequate Savior he has become through his incarnation, obedience, self-offering, and session.”  
**Locus:** L1483  
**Suggested pages:** [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[hebrews]]

### C8 — Psalms/prophets preferred as conversational divine speech
**Claim (Cockerill):** Even words originally spoken by another to, about, or on behalf of God become divine speech by inclusion in Scripture; most significant quotations come from psalms, prophets, and passages like the Song of Moses (Deut 32:1–43) because conversational. Deeper reasons: God announces the ultimate High Priest and promises the New Covenant; OT warnings take deeper significance in light of fulfillment in the Son.  
**Quote:** “Even words originally spoken by another to, about, or on behalf of God have become divine speech by being included in Scripture. Thus the pastor's most significant quotations come from the psalms, prophets, and passages like the Song of Moses in Dent 32:1-43, since these parts of the OT are conversational in nature. … First, in these passages God announces the future coming of the ultimate High Priest and promises the New Covenant. Second, God's OT words of warning take on even deeper significance in light of the fulfillment that has come in God's Son.”  
**Locus:** L1487  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[new-covenant]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C9 — Divine proclamation climaxes in Ps 110:4; New Covenant linked
**Claim (Cockerill):** God’s proclamations to Messiah/Son (Ps 2:7; 2 Sam 7:14; Ps 45:6–8; Ps 102:25–27; Ps 110:1) climax in Ps 110:4; they function as divine promise that the exalted Son will fulfill and replace the Aaronic priesthood. Jer 31:31–34 is closely related, especially to Ps 110:4: new-priest proclamation shows Aaronic ineffectiveness and Christ’s competency; New Covenant promise shows Old Covenant insufficiency and new efficacy. Ps 110:4 and Jer 31:31–34 are the key divine proclamations for fulfillment by first coming and session (Ps 110:1a). Hag 2:6 (final judgment) is fulfilled at return when enemies become footstool (Ps 110:1b).  
**Quote:** “God's proclamations to his Messiah/Son in Ps 2:7; 2 Sam 7:14; Ps 45:6-8; Ps 102:25-27; and Ps 110:1 (Heb 1:5, 8-14) reach their climax in Ps 110:4 (Heb 5:5-6; 7:1-25). … These quotations, climaxing in the proclamation of Ps 110:4, function as the divine promise that God's exalted Son will fulfill and replace the Aaronic priesthood (Heb 7:11-19). … God's New Covenant promise in Jer 31:31-34 (Heb 8:7-13; 10:15-18) is closely related to this divine conversation and especially to God's declaration of priesthood in Ps 110:4. … Thus Ps 110:4, the climax of God's conversation with his Son, and Jer 31:31-34 are the key divine proclamations upon which the pastor builds his case for the fulfillment accomplished by Christ's first coming and subsequent session (Ps 110:1a in Heb 1:13). God's promise of final judgment in Hag 2:6 (Heb 12:26) will be fulfilled at Christ's return when God makes the Son's \"enemies\" his \"footstool\" (Ps I10:1b in Heb 1:13).”  
**Locus:** L1489–L1491  
**Suggested pages:** [[melchizedek]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[new-covenant]], [[hebrews]]

### C10 — Son answers Father from Scripture; intensified urgency of obedience
**Claim (Cockerill):** The Son uses Scripture to answer the Father — incarnation (Isa 8:17–18), faithful obedience (Ps 40:6–8), vindication (Ps 22:22). Divine speech showing the present as between fulfillment and final Judgment contextualizes warnings; OT exhortations continue (Ps 95; Hab 2:3–4; Hag 2:6; Deut 31:6; Prov 3:11–13), intensified rather than nullified by the Son’s revelation. Last word to the people is promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Josh 1:5 in Heb 13:5); fitting response is Ps 118:6 (Heb 13:6).  
**Quote:** “The Son uses the words of Scripture to answer the Father. He has confirmed his acceptance of the divine invitation and the fulfillment of this promise through his incarnation (Isa 8:17, 18 in Heb 2:13), faithful obedience (Ps 40:6-8 in Heb 10:5-10), and resultant vindication (Ps 22:22 in Heb 2:12). … Second, the Intensified Urgency of Obedience. … First, since God's desire for faithful obedience is unchanging, his words of exhortation to his people of old continue to address his people in the present (Ps 95:7-11 in Heb 3:7-4:11; Hab 2:3-4 in Heb 10:37-38; Hag 2:6 in 12:25-29; Dent 31:6 in Heb 13:5). … Second, God's final revelation in his Son has intensified rather than nullified the urgency of these exhortations. … However, God's last word to his people is one of promise: \"I will never leave you nor forsake you\" (Josh 1:5 in Heb 13:5). … \"The LORD is my helper; I will not fear. What can a human being do to me?\" (Ps 118:6 quoted in Heb 13:6).”  
**Locus:** L1489–L1493

### C11 — Moses bears witness (3:5); four ways Pentateuch functions
**Claim (Cockerill):** The five Books of Moses are foundational; through describing the Old Covenant and early history of God’s people Moses bears “witness to the things that would be spoken” by God in his Son (3:5). Moses’ witness functions in at least four ways: first two support all other OT uses; third and fourth correspond to and supplement the two uses of psalms/related material.  
**Quote:** “In the psalms and prophets and related material God (1) promises the fulfillment that has come in Christ and (2) urges his people to faithful perseverance. … Through describing the Old Covenant and through relating the early history of God's people Moses bears \"witness to the things that would be spoken\" by God in his Son (3:5). Moses' witness functions in at least four different ways.”  
**Locus:** L1497  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[typology]], [[tabernacle]]

### C12 — Sinai, Promised Land, and Tent as interlocking typology
**Claim (Cockerill):** Three interlocking Pentateuch images — Sinai, the Promised Land, and the wilderness Tent — provide categories for describing Christ’s all-sufficiency and the people’s situation. Sinai is fundamental (self-revelation, fellowship). God’s self-revelation in the Son fulfills Sinai’s intention (1:1–2:18; 12:4–29); provision enables entrance to the heavenly homeland (3:1–4:13; 10:19–12:3); meanwhile daily access to the true Most Holy Place through the Son’s high priesthood (4:14–10:18). Heavenly homeland and true Most Holy Place represent the same reality — the true dwelling place of God.  
**Quote:** “First, three interlocking Pentateuch images - Sinai, the Promised Land, and the wilderness Tent - provide the categories for describing Christ's all-sufficiency and the resulting situation of God's people. Sinai is fundamental, since it was the defining mo ment of God's self-revelation when he brought his people into fellowship with himself. … God's selfrevelation in his Son has fulfilled the intention of God's self-disclosure on Sinai (1:1-2:18; 12:4-29). By its provision God's people can enter the heavenly homeland that has always been the goal of their journey (3:1-4:13; 10:1912:3). In the meantime they have daily access to God in the true Most Holy Place through the high priesthood of the Son (4:14-10:18). The heavenly homeland and the true Most Holy Place represent the same reality - the true dwelling place of God.”  
**Locus:** L1499  
**Suggested pages:** [[tabernacle]], [[promised-land]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[typology]], [[hebrews]]

### C13 — Supporting Pentateuch quotations and allusions
**Claim (Cockerill):** Short quotes/allusions from the Pentateuch clarify OT institutions/examples and explain other OT quotations: Exod 24:8 (9:20); Exod 25:40 (8:5); perhaps Deut 9:19 (12:21); Num 12:7 alluded (3:2); Gen 22:16–17 (6:14); Gen 21:12 (11:18); Gen 2:2 (4:4) to explain Ps 95:11; Gen 14:17–24 alluded (7:1–10) to explain Ps 110:4. Heb 11:1–40 is filled with biblical allusions.  
**Quote:** “Thus he quotes Exod 24:8 (Heb 9:20); Exod 25:40 (Heb 8:5); and perhaps Dent 9:19 (Heb 12:21) to clarify the descriptions of Old Covenant institutions. Note also the allusion to Num 12:7 in Heb 3:2. He quotes Gen 22:16-17 (Heb 6:14) and Gen 21:12 (Heb 11:18) in order to elucidate the example of Abraham. … Finally, the pastor quotes Gen 2:2 (Heb 4:4) in order to explain Ps 95:11, and alludes to Gen 14:17-24 (Heb 7:1-10) in order to explain Ps 110:4.”  
**Locus:** L1501

### C14 — Typological nature of the old order: correspondence and inadequacy
**Claim (Cockerill):** Pentateuchal descriptions provide both basis for correspondence with Christ’s work and signs of the old order’s inability to provide salvation. The old foreshadowed salvation as entrance into God’s presence through cleansing by effective sacrifice and competent high priest administering a covenant; inadequacy shown by earthly Tent only, once a year, only for the high priest. Together psalms/prophets’ promises and Pentateuchal descriptions establish typology: earlier work foreshadowed fulfillment it could not provide.  
**Quote:** “Third, the Pentateuchal descriptions of the old order provide both the basis for its correspondence with the work of Christ and the signs of its own inadequacy to provide salvation (Heb 5:1-3, 7-9; 8:3-5; 9:1-10, 16-22; 12:18-21). For example, the old order foreshadowed Christ by showing that salvation consisted of entrance into the presence of God through cleansing from sin by an effective sacrifice and a competent high priest who would administer a covenant. On the other hand, its inability to provide the salvation it prefigured was adequately demonstrated by the fact that it provided entrance to only an earthly Tent, only once a year, and only for the high priest. … Thus together the promises of the psalms and prophets and the descriptions in the Pentateuch establish the typological relationship between the old order and the That earlier work of God foreshadowed the fulfillment that it was not able to provide.”  
**Locus:** L1503  
**Suggested pages:** [[typology]], [[tabernacle]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C15 — OT examples of faithfulness and disobedience
**Claim (Cockerill):** Moses’ books record God’s dealings with the faithful from Abel through Abraham to Moses (Heb 11) and the disobedience of Esau (12:14–17) and the wilderness generation (3:7–4:11). The faithful embody the people of God with whom hearers should identify; the disobedient are apostates to avoid. Examples join psalms/prophets exhortations with redoubled intensity since the Son’s coming.  
**Quote:** “In addition to descriptions of the old order, the Books of Moses provide a record of God's dealings with his faithful people from Abel through Abraham to Moses (Heb 11:1-40). They also describe the disobedience and ultimate loss of Esau (12:14-17) and of the faithless wilderness generation (3:7-4:11). The faithful of old provide more than an example of persevering obedience; they embody the people of God with whom the pastor would have his hearers identify. The disobedient are the apostate whose company they must avoid.”  
**Locus:** L1505

### C16 — Historical books thin; Eisenbaum on land institutions absent from Heb 11
**Claim (Cockerill reporting Eisenbaum; Cockerill’s synthesis):** Only 2 Sam 7:14 (Heb 1:5) and (probably) Josh 1:5 (Heb 13:6) are quotations from the historical books, both functioning with psalms/related passages. Pamela Eisenbaum showed that institutions characteristic of Israel as a nation in the land play no role in Heb 11:1–40; ultimate goal is the heavenly city. Pastor never uses “Promised Land” for ultimate goal; with 4:8 dismisses notion Joshua gave ultimate “rest.” Closest typological use of earthly institutions: “heavenly Jerusalem” (12:22). Omission is theological and rhetorical: focus on Pentateuch to show Christ fulfills founding covenant; land/institutions would distract from pilgrimage to true “rest” and from rhetorical unity.  
**Quote:** “2 Samuel 7:14 (Heb 1:5) and (probably) Josh 1:5 (Heb 13:6) are the pastor's only quotations from the historical books. … Pamela Eisenbaum, however, has done interpreters of Hebrews a service by demonstrating that the institutions characteristic of Israel as a nation in the land play no role in Heb 11:1-40. The ultimate goal is the heavenly city. … The pastor never uses the term \"Promised Land\" for the ultimate goal of God's people. With one verse (4:8) he dismisses any fleeting notion that Joshua may have given God's people ultimate \"rest\" by entering that earthly entity. The closest the pastor gets to using any of these earthly institutions typologically is when he calls the eternal city the \"heavenly Jerusalem\" (12:22). … First, if he would demonstrate the finality of Christ, he must focus on the Pentateuch so that he can show how Christ fulfills the covenant upon which the people of God were founded. Second, reference to the land and its institutions would only have distracted from his insistence that the people of God have always been on pilgrimage to the true promised \"rest.\""  
**Locus:** L1509  
**Suggested pages:** [[promised-land]], [[hebrews]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]]

### C17 — Ps 95 in 3:7–4:11: blend of exhortation, example, and eschatology
**Claim (Cockerill):** Interpretation of Ps 95:7–11 in Heb 3:7–4:11 uniquely blends features: continuing exhortation from psalms; Pentateuchal example (prepared by Num 12:7 allusion, echoes Num 14, elucidated by Gen 2:2). From Davidic dating after wilderness generation: (1) OT exhortations continue “today”; (2) true destiny always future heavenly “rest,” not earthly Promised Land. Thus Ps 95 takes on eschatological character of Ps 110:1, 4 and Jer 31:31–34 — not merely exhortation but exposition fundamental to fulfillment in Christ.  
**Quote:** “The interpretation of Ps 95:7-11 in Heb 3:7-4:11 is a unique blend of several features already mentioned. First, it is an exhortation to God's people of old drawn from the psalms because of its continuing relevance. It is also, however, an example taken from the Pentateuch. … First, God's OT exhortations have continuing relevance for the people of God \"today\" (Heb 3:7). Second, the true destiny of God's people has always been a future heavenly \"rest\" and not an earthly Promised Land (Heb 4:1-11). By demonstrating this fact Ps 95:7-11 takes on the eschatological character of Ps 110:1, 4 and Jer 31:31-34. Thus this passage is not merely exhortation but exposition fundamental to the pastor's understanding of fulfillment in Christ.”  
**Locus:** L1513  
**Suggested pages:** [[promised-land]], [[hebrews]], [[typology]]

### C18 — Melchizedek neither type nor obsolete institution; Aaron is the type
**Claim (Cockerill):** Melchizedek of Gen 14:17–24 stands above both faithful history and Old Covenant institutions — neither example to follow nor antiquated institution. Function determined by Ps 110:4. Genesis appearance explains eternal nature of the coming priest and provides historical basis for superiority over Levitical priesthood. **Aaron is the type Christ fulfilled; Melchizedek provides Scriptural evidence for that fulfillment.** Without Melchizedek no adequate Scriptural substantiation for the Son’s high priesthood.  
**Quote:** “The Melchizedek of Genesis stands above both the history of the faithful and the institutions of the Old Covenant. … Melchizedek is neither an example to be followed nor an institution of the old order now antiquated by the coming of God's Son. His function in Hebrews is determined by Ps 110:4 (Heb 5:6, 10; 6:20; 7:17, 21). … Aaron is the type which Christ has fulfilled. Melchizedek provides the Scriptural evidence for Christ's fulfillment of the Aaronic priesthood. … Without him there would be no adequate Scriptural substantiation for the high priesthood of the Son.”  
**Locus:** L1515  
**Suggested pages:** [[melchizedek]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[typology]], [[hebrews]]

### C19 — Heb 12:18–24 as full fruition: Sinai for apostate, Zion for faithful
**Claim (Cockerill):** If Melchizedek is the seed making interpretation possible, Heb 12:18–24 is full fruition. “Sinai” (12:18–21) and “Zion” (12:22–24) represent what Sinai has become for apostate then faithful. Because the Son fulfilled the Sinai type per OT promises, the faithful enjoy God’s presence on “Zion”; for apostates, Sinai of exclusion without grace. Warning climaxes use of Ps 95 and other exhortations. Fulfillment clarified typological nature of sacrificial ritual but intensified demand for faithful obedience.  
**Quote:** “If Melchizedek is the seed that makes the pastor's interpretation possible, then Heb 12:18-24 is its full fruition. The \"Sinai\" of 12:18-21 and the \"Zion\" of 12:22-24 represent what Sinai has become first for the apostate, then for the faithful. … the faithful enjoy the presence of God on \"Zion.\" On the other hand, … the apostate stands before a \"Sinai\" of exclusion from God's presence reserved for those who have rejected the Son - Sinai without grace. … Christ's fulfillment of the old order has clarified the typological nature of its sacrificial ritual but intensified its demand for faithful obedience.”  
**Locus:** L1517  
**Suggested pages:** [[typology]], [[hebrews]], [[new-covenant]]

### C20 — Continuity-and-fulfillment, not continuity-and-discontinuity
**Claim (Cockerill vs. Graham Hughes and others):** Second pair of principles (examples + exhortations) affirms continuity of God’s people. Hughes represents many who treat the first pair (Pentateuchal descriptions + new-order promises) as establishing discontinuity; Cockerill rejects this as failing to hear Hebrews on its own terms. Typological relationship is continuity: OT’s own testimony shows Old Covenant never intended to be final; always typological and anticipatory. Relationship best described as **continuity and fulfillment** rather than continuity and discontinuity. “Abolished” (7:18) means faithful must no longer practice old sacrifices since Christ fulfilled them; continuing them would deny continuity through fulfillment.  
**Quote:** “Graham Hughes, however, represents many who would argue that the first pair of principles given above establishes discontinuity between the old and the new. … This ap proach, however, fails to hear Hebrews on its own terms. The typological relationship established by the first pair of principles above is one of continuity. These principles do not show that the Old Covenant has been invalidated, but that, on the basis of its own testimony, it was never intended to be final. … Thus, the relationship between Christ's high priesthood and the old is best described as continuity and fulfillment rather than continuity and discontinuity. … By this statement, as noted above, the pastor means that the faithful must no longer practice the sacrifices of the old order since Christ has fulfilled what they anticipated. To continue these practices would be to deny the continuity that Christ has established with the old through its fulfillment.”  
**Locus:** L1521–L1523  
**Suggested pages:** [[typology]], [[new-covenant]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]]

### C21 — Definition of typology; restrictions (Aaron vs Melchizedek; people not types)
**Claim (Cockerill):** Hebrews’ old/new relationship falls within general typology: OT institutions, persons, events through which God redeemed were types foreshadowing Christ; correspondence yet superior fulfillment; types supply pattern/structure/vocabulary. In Hebrews types are revelatory and anticipatory but devoid of ultimate saving efficacy. **Aaron, not Melchizedek, is a type of Christ**; because the Son is “like” Melchizedek (7:15–19) he is superior to Aaron and fulfills what Aaron foreshadowed. Using “typology” for both opposite relationships introduces confusion. OT people of God are not a type of the new — one people throughout history; faithful of 11:1–40 are examples, not types.  
**Quote:** “This relationship that Hebrews establishes between the old and new covenants and priesthoods falls within the definition generally given to the term \"typology\": OT institutions, persons, and events through which God re deemed his people were types that foreshadowed what he would accomplish in Christ. … In Hebrews, for instance, the types are revelatory and anticipatory, but devoid in themselves of ultimate saving efficacy. Furthermore, as has been noted above, Aaron, not Melchizedek, is a type of Christ. It is because the Son is \"like\" Melchizedek (Heb 7:15-19) that he is superior to Aaron and fulfills what Aaron foreshadowed. To use the word \"typology\" for both of these, all but opposite, relationships introduces naught but confusion. It is also misleading to call the OT people of God a type of the new. … The faithful of 11: 1-40 are not types but examples drawn from the earlier history of that one people.”  
**Locus:** L1525  
**Suggested pages:** [[typology]], [[melchizedek]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C22 — Parallels with contemporary Jewish exegesis (qal wahomer, gezera shawa, etc.)
**Claim (Cockerill):** Recognized general parallels with contemporary Jewish practice: lesser-to-greater (*qal wayyomer*; e.g. 2:1–4; 10:26–31; 12:25–29); associating verses with same word(s) (*gezera shawa*; e.g. “son” 1:5, “rest” 4:1–11); possible first-mention emphasis and argument from silence (Melchizedek’s missing genealogy); stringing quotations (1:5–14 like 4QFlorilegium, 4QTestimonia, 4QCatena); roll call of faithful reminiscent of Sirach 45–50. Merits evaluated in commentary.  
**Quote:** “Hebrews is fond of arguing from the lesser to the greater (in Hebrew, qal wayyomer; e.g., 2:1-4; 10:26-31; 12:25-29). Hebrews sometimes associates verses that contain the same word or words (in Hebrew, gezera shawa; e.g., \"son\" in 1:5 or \"rest\" in 4:1-11). Some have suggested that Hebrews puts special emphasis on the first mention of something in Scripture (e.g., \"rest\" in Gen 2:2/Heb 4:1-11; \"priest\" in Gen 12:14-27/Heb 7:1-10) or that Hebrews argues from the silence of Scripture (e.g., the absence of Melchizedek's genealogy in Gen 14:17-24/Heb 7:1-3). Heb 1:5-14 (like 4QFlorilegium, 4QTestimonia, and 4QCatena) strings a number of quotations together in order to sustain a particular point. The roll call of the faithful in Heb 11:1-40 is reminiscent of hero lists in Sirach 45-50 and other sources.”  
**Locus:** L1529

### C23 — Docherty/Goldberg parallels with rabbis; Cockerill’s Christological distinction
**Claim (Cockerill reporting Docherty; then critiquing):** Susan Docherty, using Arnold Goldberg’s analysis of actual rabbinic practice, finds shared features: care in quoting; associating texts across canon; new context for quotations while aware of larger context; highlighting key words; concern with textual particularities/ambiguities. What Docherty fails to see: these methods implement Christological interpretation. New context is Christological (God who spoke of old now in Son); sense of historical sequence, progression, fulfillment absent from rabbis; highlighted expressions central not peripheral; unified Christological focus. Pace Docherty, for Hebrews the OT is never the linguistic “artifact” it was for the rabbis — meaning is Christologically determined; “exalted speech,” living record of God’s actions and voice. Literary form as synagogue sermon drawing on ancient rhetoric sustains and is sustained by unified Christological vision.  
**Quote:** “According to Docherty, both Hebrews and the rabbis demonstrate their commitment to the OT as God's word by the care with which they quote its text. … What Docherty fails to see, however, is the way in which the pastor's use of these very methods distinguishes him from the rabbis. These procedures implement and give legitimacy to his Christological First, the new context into which the pastor puts OT quotations is a Christological context: the God who spoke of old has now spoken in one who is Son (cf. Heb 1:1). … Thus Hebrews has a sense of historical sequence, progression, and fulfillment absent from the rabbis. … Thus pace Docherty, for the writer of Hebrews the OT can never be the linguistic \"artifact\" that it was for the rabbis. … Its meaning is Christologically determined. It is \"exalted speech,\" the living record of the actions and the voice of God. … The way in which this synagogue sermon draws on the resources of ancient rhetoric to arrange all of its material in a unified, persuasive whole sustains, and is sustained by, the pastor's unified vision of the OT's Christological fulfillment.”  
**Locus:** L1531–L1535  
**Suggested pages:** [[gareth-lee-cockerill]], [[hebrews]]

### C24 — Contemporary relevance; Hughes’s “permission”; Cockerill’s firmer framing
**Claim (Cockerill reporting positions; own synthesis):** Some condemn the pastor’s exegesis as time-conditioned; others appeal to *sensus plenior*. Graham Hughes finds firmer basis: OT intimations of something better plus specific ways Jesus fulfilled them give “permission”; OT might “invite”/“suggest” but interpretation not necessitated without faith in Christ. Cockerill reframes: if God has not spoken in one who is Son, other interpretations are valid — but that question is far from the mind of one confident of the Son’s vocation. Pastor argues from OT alone not only for “futurity” (Hughes) but for **futility** of the old order as means of salvation; then shows coherent fulfillment. Not pesher of esoteric mysteries; God-intended fulfillment, not revision. Abiding principles: (1) word in incarnate/obedient/exalted Son fulfills all God said; (2) Old Covenant priesthood/sacrifices always type/foreshadowing, never adequate in themselves; (3) one people of God by faith, goal always eternal “rest,” examples/warnings retain validity with increased urgency. These principles do **not** warrant “critiquing and relativizing” objectionable Scriptural teachings.  
**Quote:** “Graham Hughes, however, has found a firmer basis for the pastor's exposition. He argues that the OT intimations of something better yet to come plus the specific ways in which Jesus has fulfilled these intimations give \"permission\" for the pastor to develop his interpretation. … If one were to put Hughes's position in terms more congenial to the writer of Hebrews, one might say, \"If God has not now spoken in one who is Son, other interpretations of the OT are valid.\" … On the basis of the OT alone he argues not merely for the \"futurity\" (to use Graham Hughes's term), but for the futility of the old order as a means of salvation. … The pastor does not present a revision of God's OT word, but its God-intended … First and most fundamentally, God's word in the incarnate, obedient, now exalted Son fulfills all that God has said. … Second, the Old Covenant with its priesthood and sacrifices has always been and continues to be a type and foreshadowing of the full sufficiency of Christ as Savior. … Third, those who live by faith in the word of God constitute the one people of God throughout history. … They do not, however, provide liberty for contemporary Christians to \"critique and relativize\" teachings of Scripture they might find objectionable.”  
**Locus:** L1539–L1545  
**Suggested pages:** [[typology]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]], [[hebrews]]

### C25 — Structure overview: three large sections; chiastic I || III with II center
**Claim (Cockerill):** Parallel of Heb 4:14–16 and 10:19–25 divides main body into three large sections: 1:1–4:13; 4:14–10:18; 10:19–12:29. High priesthood predominates only in the center. Section I: God’s revelation in the Son and warning against disobedience. Section II: Christ’s high priesthood as fulfillment of sonship and content of self-disclosure. Section III: faithful endurance until return, enabled by high priesthood. Reverse/chiastic parallelism between I and III, but not equal — preparation to fruition. Divine sonship is foundation; high priesthood main theme; perseverance ultimate goal. Prior structural proposals (epideictic/deliberative divisions; OT-quotation structure; Vanhoye literary features; Guthrie/Westfall discourse analysis) each have values but none fully satisfactory.  
**Quote:** “The parallel character of Heb 4:14-16 and 10:19-25 provides the initial impetus for dividing the main body of Hebrews into three large sections - 1:1-4:13; 4:14-10:18; and 10:19-12:29. Even though the high priesthood of Christ is the pastor's main theme, it predominates only in the central of these three sections. The first section proclaims God's revelation in the Son and warns against disobedience. The second presents Christ's high priesthood as the fulfillment of his sonship and the content of God's self-disclosure in the Son. … the third section urges faithful endurance until Christ's return, enabled by the sufficiency of his high priesthood. Although the comments below will show a reverse or chiastic parallelism between sections one and three, these sections are not equal. They relate to one another as preparation to fruition. The divine sonship of the first section is the pastor's foundation. The high priesthood of the Son in the second is his main theme. The perseverance of the people of God in the third is his ultimate goal.”  
**Locus:** L1551–L1555  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C26 — Sinai frame: 1:1–2:18 and 12:4–29
**Claim (Cockerill):** Pastor structures Hebrews by how the Son fulfills Sinai / Promised Land / Tent. Perseverance urged via Promised Land imagery (homeland, City, rest) in 3:1–4:13 and 10:19–12:3; present approach via heavenly Most Holy Place / Tent typology in 4:14–10:18; begins and ends comparing revelation in Son with Sinai. In 1:1–2:18 contrast of “so great salvation” spoken in Son with Sinai “word” through angels (2:1–4). Ubelacker: 1:1–4 *exordium*; 1:5–2:18 *narratio*; 2:17–18 *propositio* (central thesis: Son as all-sufficient High Priest). 2:10 introduces subsidiary Pioneer/example theme (returns at center 12:1–3 of final section). Return to Sinai vision in 12:14–29; final Judgment vs earth-shaking Sinai voice (12:25–29). Final section begins at 12:4 because Jesus in 12:1–3 turns between people past and present; correspondence of subsections 1:1–2:18 || 12:4–29.  
**Quote:** “When the pastor would urge his hearers to perseverance in 3:1-4:13 and 10:19-12:3 he uses Promised Land imagery … When he would urge them to approach God even now … he describes it as the heavenly Most Holy Place typified by the Tent (4:14-10:18). The pastor begins and ends by comparing God's ultimate self-revelation in the Son with his self-disclosure on Sinai. … Ubelacker describes Heb 1:1-4 as the exordium or introduction to an ancient speech and 1:5-2:18 as the narratio or narration of the facts the speech would present. This narratio climaxes in 2:17-18 with the thesis the orator would establish, called the propositio or proposition. … If 2:17-18 introduces the pastor's central thesis that the Son is the all-sufficient High Priest, 2:10 introduces the subsidiary theme of the Son as the Pioneer and example par excellence of endurance (12:1-3 …). … The first (High Priest) will dominate the central section of Hebrews (4:14-10:18); the second (Pioneer) surfaces again at the center (12:13) of the final section (10:19-12:29).”  
**Locus:** L1561–L1567  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[tabernacle]], [[promised-land]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C27 — Pilgrimage blocks 3:1–4:13 and 10:19–12:3; strategic placement of means
**Claim (Cockerill):** After Sinai fulfillment assertion, natural to warn against wilderness generation (3:1–4:13); sequel is invitation to join obedient on pilgrimage (11:1–12:3). Between them: full sufficiency of High Priest (4:14–10:18). More effective to put what to avoid before what to embrace; means of perseverance between the two is strategic. Extend invitation section back to 10:19; attach 4:14–16 and 10:19–25 to what follows. 10:19–39 is three-link chain binding 11:1–12:3 to 4:14–10:18: benefits (10:19–25); neglect warning (10:26–31); invitation to join faithful (10:32–39). Detailed chiastic correspondences: 10:19–25 || 4:14–16; 10:26–31 || 4:12–13; 10:32–39 || 4:1–11; 11:1–40 vs 3:7–19; 3:1–6 trajectory to 12:1–3 Pioneer.  
**Quote:** “Thus after warning his hearers to shun the wilderness generation (3:1-4:13) the pastor proclaims the full sufficiency of Christ their High Priest (4:14-10:18) before urging them to join the faithful (11:1-12:3). He knows that it is more effective to put what he would have his hearers avoid before what he would have them embrace. … In fact, 10:19-39 as a whole is best understood as a three-link chain binding the history of the faithful in 11:112:3 to the sufficiency of Christ as High Priest in 4:14-10:18. The first link urges perseverance based on the great benefits available in Christ (10:19-25); the second warns of the dire consequences for neglecting these benefits (10:26-31); and the third is an invitation to exercise such perseverance by joining the faithful people of God (10:32-39) as described in 11:1-12:3. … the history of the faithful of old in 11:1-40 stands in opposition to the history of the disobedient wilderness generation in 3:7 19. Finally, the introduction of Christ as the faithful Son in 3:1-6 sets a trajectory toward the climactic presentation of Christ as \"the Pioneer and Perfecter of the faith\" and example par excellence of suffering in 12:1-3.”  
**Locus:** L1575–L1589  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C28 — Macro-chiasm: History of Disobedient (I) || History of Faithful (III)
**Claim (Cockerill):** 1:1–4:13 = “A Short History of the Disobedient”; 10:19–12:29 = “A History of the Faithful People of God from Creation to Consummation.” Chiastic but unequal: A/B under I given for sake of B′/A′ under III; Christ High Priest at center (II) is turning point. As High Priest, eternal/incarnate/exalted Son fulfills all-sufficient Savior (A); clarifies severity of 3:1–4:13 (B); provides means to emulate faithful (B′); provides present access and eternal destiny (A′). Arrangement demonstrates tight integration of “expository” and “hortatory” parts.  
**Quote:** “Heb 1:1-4:13 is \"A Short History of the Disobedient\"; Heb 10:19-12:29 is \"A History of the Faithful People of God from Creation to Consummation.\" … The pastor begins in \"A\" by presenting the foundation of what he will teach about Christ and salvation. He follows this foundation in \"B\" with the example he would have his hearers avoid. After explaining the high priesthood of Christ (\"II\"), he presents the grand history of the examples he would have them emulate (\"B1\"), followed by the ultimate destiny of the people of God (\"Ai\"). Thus \"A\"/`B\" under \"I\" and \"B\"\"/\"Ai\" under \"III\" are chiastic but not equal. The first pair are given for the sake of the second. Christ the only effective High Priest at the center (\"II\") is the turning point that is crucial to the whole. … this arrangement demonstrates the tight integration between the supposed expository and hortatory parts of Hebrews.”  
**Locus:** L1593–L1607  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C29 — Chapter 13 as peroration and letter ending
**Claim (Cockerill):** Heb 13:1–21(18?) is the *peroratio*/peroration with which ancient orators concluded; final attempt to make message concrete. Letter-ending 13:22(19?)–25 shows the sermon was sent to be read to the congregation and confirms use in modern Christian worship.  
**Quote:** “Heb 13:1-21(18?) can be appropriately described as the peroratio or peroration with which ancient orators were wont to conclude their This section is the pastor's final attempt to make his message concrete in the lives of his hearers. The letterending in 13:22(19?)-25 shows that this sermon was sent to be read to the congregation and thus confirms its use in the worship of modern Christians.”  
**Locus:** L1611  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C30 — Central section 4:14–10:18: Aaron comparison, Ps 110:4, preparation digression
**Claim (Cockerill):** Central section develops theme introduced in 2:17–18 — sole sufficiency of Christ as High Priest. 4:14–16 introduction arouses curiosity. Immediately then comparison/contrast Aaronic priest and Christ (5:1–10); at heart 5:5–6 biblical evidence Ps 110:4; concludes “high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.” Before continuing explanation: shame for immaturity (5:11–6:3); apostasy warning (6:4–8); assurance not fallen (6:9–12); urge trust in oath-backed promise fulfilled by high-priestly entrance (6:13–20).  
**Quote:** “The vital central section of Hebrews describes the theme that was first introduced in 2:17-18, the sole sufficiency of Christ as High Priest. … immediately after the introduction in 4:14-16 the pastor provides a comparison/contrast between the Aaronic priest and Christ (5:1-10). … At the heart of this comparison/contrast in 5:5-6 the pastor presents the biblical evidence for Christ's replacement of Aaron - Ps 110:4. … Thus before continuing with his explanation of Christ's high priesthood he seeks to awaken them from their laxity and spiritual regression. He first shames them for their immaturity (5:11-6:3); then he warns them of the dire consequences awaiting the once \"enlightened\" who fall away (6:4-8). … Finally, he urges them to join those like Abraham who live trusting in the certainty of the oath-backed promise of God now fulfilled by Christ's high-priestly entrance into God's presence (6:13-20).”  
**Locus:** L1615–L1617  
**Suggested pages:** [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[melchizedek]], [[hebrews]]

### C31 — Heb 7: Ps 110:4 via Gen 14; legitimacy, eternity, then sacrifice intro
**Claim (Cockerill):** God who invited “sit at my right hand” (Ps 110:1) pronounced “priest forever after the order of Melchizedek” (v. 4). 7:1–10: Gen 14 shows Melchizedek greater than Levi/Aaron’s father. 7:11–19: Ps 110:4 substantiates replacement of Aaron by eternal Son. 7:20–25: certainty/sufficiency based on God’s oath and Son’s eternity. 7:26–28 summarizes and introduces sacrifice theme (how eternal Son became High Priest through suffering/self-offering as in 2:5–18).  
**Quote:** “In Heb 7:1-10 the pastor turns to Gen 14:17-24 in order to show that Melchizedek was greater than Levi, the father of Aaron. In 7:11-19 he shows how Ps 110:4 substantiates the replacement of Aaron by the eternal Son. In 7:20-25 he outlines the certainty and sufficiency of Christ's priesthood because it is based on both the oath of God and the eternity of the Son. … Thus in Heb 7:26-28 he summarizes what he has already said and introduces this theme of sacrifice.”  
**Locus:** L1619  
**Suggested pages:** [[melchizedek]], [[priesthood-of-christ]]

### C32 — “Symphony” 8:1–10:18: three movements × sanctuary / sacrifice / covenant
**Claim (Cockerill):** Heb 8:1–10:18 is the pastor’s grand “symphony” on Christ’s sacrifice in three movements (8:1–13; 9:1–22; 9:23–10:18), each repeating the same three themes in the same order — sanctuary (8:1–2; 9:1–10; 9:23–24); sacrifice (8:3–5; 9:11–15; 9:25–10:14); covenant (8:6–13; 9:16–22; 10:15–18). Purpose: progressively reveal ultimate quality of Christ’s sacrifice. First movement: OT prophecies of the new. Second: foreshadowings and inadequacy of old-order descriptions. Third: full description of sufficiency and reasons for effectiveness. Sacrifice sections increase in size; present self-offering as true Day of Atonement removing sin, also high-priestly consecration seating him at God’s right, and sacrifice establishing him Guarantor/Mediator of New Covenant.  
**Quote:** “Hebrews 8:1-10:18 is the pastor's grand \"symphony\" on the sacrifice of Christ. This symphony consists of three movements (8:1-13; 9:1-22; 9:2310:18), in each of which the pastor repeats the same three themes in the same order - sanctuary (8:1-2; 9:1-10; 9:23-24); sacrifice (8:3-5; 9:11-15; 9:2510:14); and covenant (8:6-13; 9:16-22; 10:15-18). The purpose of this symphony is progressively to reveal the ultimate quality of Christ's sacrifice. The first movement initiates this process by focusing on the OT prophecies of the new. The second carries this concern further by looking at both the foreshadowings revealed by and the inadequacy inherent in the descriptions of the old order within the OT. The third concludes by giving a full description of the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice and the reasons for its effectiveness. Note the increasing size of the sacrifice section at the center of each movement (8:3-5; 9:11-15; 9:25-10:14). … Because it has removed sin, it is also the sacrifice of high-priestly consecration through which he has taken his seat at God's right (8:1-2; 9:1-10; 9:23-24) and the sacrifice by which he has established and become Guarantor/Mediator of the New Covenant (8:6-13; 9:1622; 10:15-18).”  
**Locus:** L1621  
**Suggested pages:** [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[new-covenant]], [[tabernacle]], [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C33 — Central section outline (4:14–10:18) as Cockerill structures it
**Claim (Cockerill):** Outline of II: A. Introduction “We have such a High Priest” (4:14–5:10); B. Preparation: Don’t Fail to Grasp This Truth (5:11–6:20); C. His Legitimacy and Eternity (7:1–28); D. All-Sufficient Sacrifice: Symphony in Three Movements (8:1–10:18) — First: New Promised (8:1–13); Second: Old Antiquated, New Foreshadowed (9:1–22); Third: New Explained (9:23–10:18).  
**Quote:** “II. The Son's All-Sufficient High Priesthood (4:14-10:18) A. Introduction: \"We have such a High Priest\" (4:14-5:10) … B. Preparation: Don't Fail to Grasp This Truth (5:11-6:20) … C. His Legitimacy and Eternity (7:1-28) … D. His All-Sufficient Sacrifice: A Symphony in Three Movements (8:1-10:18) • First Movement: The New Promised (8:1-13) • Second Movement: The Old Antiquated; the New Foreshadowed (9:1-22) • Third Movement: The New Explained (9:23-10:18)”  
**Locus:** L1623–L1657

### C34 — Ps 110:1 as spine unifying structure and OT exposition
**Claim (Cockerill):** Ps 110:1’s pervasive influence accords with early Christian tradition. Central to foundation 1:1–2:18; returns 8:1–2 at heart of high-priesthood section; surfaces 12:1–3 at turning point of faithful history. “Sit at my right hand” (1:13) at center of introduction anticipates “You have come to Mount Zion” (12:22) at center of conclusion. In peroration, pastor stunnningly replaces expected Ps 110:1 reference with Jesus’ suffering “outside the gate” (13:12). Explains Ps 110:1 via Ps 110:4, Ps 40:6–8, and Jer 31:31–34 in developing tradition toward high priesthood and New Covenant.  
**Quote:** “The pervasive influence of Ps 110:1 is in accord with the pastor's dependence on early Christian tradition. This verse is central to the foundation that the pastor lays in 1:1-2:18. It returns in 8:1-2 to play a crucial role at the heart of the central section on Christ's high priesthood (4:14-10:18). It surfaces again in 12:1-3 at the turning point in the concluding history of the faithful (10: 19-12:29). \"Sit at my right hand\" in 1:13 at the center of the introduction (1:1-2:18) anticipates \"You have come to Mount Zion\" in 12:22, at the center of the conclusion to the main body of this sermon (12:4-29). In a stunning but most effective way the pastor replaces the expected reference to this verse in the peroration with Jesus' suffering \"outside the gate\" (13:12). The pastor's explanation of Ps 110:1 in terms of Ps 110:4; Ps 40:6-8; and Jer 31:31-34 is in harmony with the way he develops Christian tradition in terms of Christ's high priesthood and the New Covenant.”  
**Locus:** L1663  
**Suggested pages:** [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[new-covenant]], [[hebrews]], [[melchizedek]]

### C35 — OT quotation distribution across three major sections
**Claim (Cockerill):** 1:1–2:18 dominated by Ps 110:1 (alluded 1:3; quoted 1:13; explained via Ps 8, Ps 22, Isa 8:17–18 in 2:5–18); session-to-return interval contextualizes Ps 95 warning in 3:1–4:13. Central section: first half (4:14–7:28) dominated by Ps 110:4; second (8:1–10:18) by Ps 40:6–8; Jer 31:31–34 foundation for 8:1–10:18, Ps 40:6–8 its goal; Son answers Ps 110:4 with Ps 40:6–8 as he answered Ps 110:1 with Ps 22 / Isa 8 in ch. 2; returns to Ps 110:1 in 10:11–14 for seated Son as New Covenant mediator. Faithful history (10:19–12:29): first half dominated by Hab 2:3–4; 12:1–3 reintroduces Christ per Ps 110:1; last half features Prov 3:11–12 and Hag 2:6; center “You have come to Mount Zion” (12:18–24) as result of session.  
**Quote:** “Since 1:1-2:18 lays the foundation for what follows, it is no surprise that this passage is dominated by Ps 110:1. … The time between the session of Christ in the first half of this verse and his return in the second provides the context for the warning from Ps 95:7-11 in Heb 3:1-4:13. The central section on Christ's high priesthood (Heb 4:14-10:18) attests the high-priestly nature of the session to which the Son was invited in Ps 110:1 (Heb 8:1-2). The first half of this section (4:14-7:28) is dominated by Ps 110:4; the second (8:1-10:18), by Ps 40:6-8. Jer 31:31-34 (Heb 8:7-13; 10:15-18) provides the foundation for the argument of Heb 8:1-10:18, but Ps 40:6-8 (Heb 10:5-10) is its goal. … The first half of this history (10:19-12:3) is dominated by Hab 2:3-4 (Heb 10:37-39) … The last half of this history features both the exhortation to endure suffering as God's formative discipline in Prov 3:11-12 (Heb 12:4-17) and the promise of final Judgment from Hag 2:6 (Heb 12:25-29). Note the pastor's declaration at the center of this section: \"You have come to Mount Zion\" (12:18-24).”  
**Locus:** L1665–L1671  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[new-covenant]]

### C36 — Engagement with ancient rhetoric (Ubelacker) beyond handbook labels
**Claim (Cockerill):** Analysis accords with author drawing on ancient rhetoric to communicate truth and move hearers. Structuring accords with Ubelacker’s identification of 1:1–4 *exordium*; 1:5–2:18 *narratio*/conceptual foundation; 2:17–18 *propositio*/main proposition; and 13:1–21(18) as peroration. Analysis does more than identify similarities: provides basis for understanding how pastor effectively carried out persuasion.  
**Quote:** “The above analysis is in full accord with the suggestion that the author of Hebrews has drawn on the resources of ancient rhetoric in order to communicate the truth and move his hearers to action. Suggestions as to the relationship between various sections of Hebrews and the parts of an address described by contemporary handbooks on rhetoric vary. The structuring proposed above is in accord with Ubelacker's identification of 1:1-2:18 as the pastor's exordium or introduction (1:1-4); narratio or conceptual foundation (1:5-2:18); and propositio or main \"proposition\" (2:17-18). It has also identified 13:1-21(18) as the peroration or concluding appeal. The above analysis, however, does more than identify similarities with ancient rhetoric. It provides a basis for understanding how the pastor has effectively carried out his program of persuasion.”  
**Locus:** L1687  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[gareth-lee-cockerill]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C37 — Abiding message summary: God has spoken; persevere via High Priest
**Claim (Cockerill):** For God’s people in a world refusing to acknowledge God: God has spoken; Scripture’s words valid; incarnation, suffering, obedience, self-offering, exaltation of eternal Son are ultimate self-disclosure fulfilling what went before and all-sufficient provision for entering presence through cleansing; mediated through seated Son; invite drawing near; life on certainty of promise and power for present victory; persevere despite world’s opposition until return; for those turning aside in rebellion/unbelief, invitation becomes ultimate judgment.  
**Quote:** “Hebrews has a message for the people of God who live in a world that refuses to acknowledge God: God has spoken. The words of Scripture are valid. The incarnation, suffering, obedience, self-offering, and exaltation of God's eternal Son are the ultimate self-disclosure of the divine character fulfilling what has gone before. They are also the all-sufficient provision for entering God's presence through cleansing from sin. This revelation of God and these benefits are now mediated through the incarnate, exalted, eternal Son seated at God's right. … For those who turn aside in rebellion and unbelief due to a desire for the world's approval or fear of its ire, the divine word of invitation will become a word of ultimate judgment.”  
**Locus:** L1691  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C38 — High priesthood not mere rhetorical device; Aaron is the metaphor
**Claim (Cockerill):** Message remains valid; high priesthood is intrinsic to Son’s identity as Savior and Revealer — cannot be reduced to a rhetorical device useful for addressing hearers. **Aaron is the metaphor; the Son is the true “Great High Priest” (4:14).** Reality based on Scripture (7:1–28); significance encompasses full scope of work (incarnation, obedience, exaltation); provides full repertoire of benefits (curse deliverance, forgiveness, cleansing, law on heart, present/ultimate access); fulfills OT sacrifices multiply as atonement, consecration, New Covenant guarantee. Force of argument depends on Son as High Priest *par excellence*.  
**Quote:** “Because high priesthood is intrinsic to the Son's identity as both all-sufficient Savior and Revealer, it cannot be reduced to a rhetorical device useful for addressing the hearers. Aaron is the metaphor; the Son is the true \"Great High Priest\" (4:14). The pastor establishes the reality of the Son's high priesthood by basing it on Scripture (7:1-28). The significance of his priesthood is demonstrated by the way in which it encompasses the full scope of his work - incarnation, obedience, and exaltation (7:1-10:18, esp. 10:5-10). As High Priest the Son provides a full repertoire of benefits - deliverance from the covenant curse, forgiveness, cleansing, God's law implanted in the heart, present access to God, ultimate entrance into his presence. … The force of the author's argument depends on the Son's being the High Priest par excellence.”  
**Locus:** L1693  
**Suggested pages:** [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[typology]], [[new-covenant]], [[hebrews]]

### C39 — Authentic cleansing and access; conscience defilement vs ritual impurity
**Claim (Cockerill):** Appeal would lose effectiveness without authentic cleansing from sin and true entrance through genuine high priesthood. As Aaron was metaphor for Christ’s priesthood, Old Covenant ritual defilement was metaphor for moral/spiritual defilement of heart/conscience. Ritual impurity debarred from Mosaic Tent worship; disobedient/rebellious heart separates from congregation and prevents present/final entrance. By obedient self-offering the High Priest redeemed from covenant curse (9:16–22); cleansed consciences from dead works (9:10–14) so approach with true hearts (10:22); empowered persevering obedience by inscribing law on hearts (10:15–18). Great concern: hearers persevere by drawing near (4:14–16; 10:19–25).  
**Quote:** “Furthermore, the pastor's appeal would lose its effectiveness if the people of God could not experience an authentic cleansing from sin and a true entrance into the divine presence through the Son's genuine high priesthood. As Aaron was a metaphor for Christ's high priesthood, so the ritual defilement of the Old Covenant was a metaphor for the moral and spiritual defilement of the heart or conscience. … By his obedient self-offering Christ the High Priest that \"we have\" (4:14; 10:21) has redeemed his people from the covenant curse acquired by their sin (9:16-22); \"cleansed their consciences from dead works\" (9:10-14) so that they can approach God with \"true hearts\" and purified lives (10:22); and empowered them for persevering obedience under the new covenant by inscribing God's law on their hearts (10:15-18). The pastor's great concern is that all who hear his voice continue to persevere by availing themselves of the grace provided by drawing near to God through this effective High Priest (4:14-16; 10: 19-25).”  
**Locus:** L1695  
**Suggested pages:** [[new-covenant]], [[priesthood-of-christ]], [[hebrews]]

### C40 — Full sermon outline (Parts I–IV) with chiastic cross-references
**Claim (Cockerill):** Outline organizing the commentary:  
**I.** Very Short History of the Disobedient (1:1–4:13): A. Sinai Revisited (1:1–2:18: 1:1–4; 1:5–14; 2:1–4; 2:5–18); B. Tested at Kadesh-Barnea (3:1–4:13: 3:1–6; 3:7–19; 4:1–11; 4:12–13).  
**II.** Son’s High Priesthood — Resource and Urgency (4:14–10:18): A. 4:14–5:10; B. 5:11–6:20; C. 7:1–28; D. Symphony 8:1–10:18 (three movements).  
**III.** History of the Faithful from Creation to Consummation (10:19–12:29), with parenthetical chiastic parallels to Part I (and II.A.1): 10:19–25 || II.A.1; 10:26–31 || I.B.4; 10:32–39 || I.B.3; 11:1–40 || I.B.2; 12:1–3 || I.B.1; 12:4–13 || I.A.4; 12:14–17 || I.A.3; 12:18–24 || I.A.2; 12:25–29 || I.A.1.  
**IV.** Instructions for Life of Gratitude and Godly Fear (13:1–25): community (13:1–6); unbelieving world (13:7–17); sermon sent as letter (13:18–25).  
**Quote:** “An outline of Hebrews based on the above structural analysis is given below as an aid to the reader of this commentary. … The numbers in parentheses following the sub-headings of Part III designate the corresponding sections in Part I (and Part II, A, 1) with which the subheadings of Part III are chiastically parallel. 1. A Very Short History of the Disobedient People of God (1:1-4:13) … II. The Son's High Priesthood - Resource and Urgency for Perseverance (4:14-10:18) … III. A History of the Faithful People of God from Creation to Consummation (10: 19-12:29) … 1. Avail Yourselves of This Great Priest (10:19-25) (II, A, 1) 2. You Are More Accountable because of This High Priest (10:26-31) (I, B, 4) … 4. God Will Speak \"Once More\" at the Final Judgment (12:2529) (I, A, 1) IV. Instructions for the Life of Gratitude and Godly Fear (13:1-25)”  
**Locus:** L1699–L1789  
**Suggested pages:** [[hebrews]], [[cockerill-hebrews-nicnt]]

### C41 — Critique of rival structural analyses (Vanhoye, Westfall, Guthrie)
**Claim (Cockerill):** Vanhoye’s literary-features-only approach seems artificial; forcing Hebrews into chiastic mold breaks down in the central section. Westfall’s claim that Jesus is speaker of Psalm 95 in 3:7–4:11, essential to her structure, finds no support in the text. Guthrie would have been more helpful analyzing expository and hortatory sections as a unity; each hortatory section crafted for a particular place in the sermon.  
**Quote:** “Vanhoye's insistence on using literary features alone seems artificial. His attempt to force Hebrews into a chiastic mold breaks down in the central section of the book. Westfall's insistence that Jesus is the speaker of Psalm 95 in Heb 3:7-4:11, while essential to her structural analysis, finds no support in the text. Guthrie's insightful work would have been more helpful had he analyzed the expository and hortatory sections as a unity. As the paragraphs below in particular and the text of this commentary in general hope to demonstrate, each hortatory section has been crafted to fit a particular place in the”  
**Locus:** L1553  
**Suggested pages:** [[gareth-lee-cockerill]], [[hebrews]]

### C42 — Notes on coherence of 4:14–7:28 and transitional 10:19–39
**Claim (Cockerill, footnotes embedded in structure discussion):** Ps 110:4 gives 4:14–7:28 certain coherence (announced at heart of 5:1–10; exhortation 5:11–6:20 leads into 7:1–28), yet 5:1–10 also announces themes for 8:1–10:18; helpful to divide central section into four main parts (4:14–5:10; 5:11–6:20; 7:1–28; 8:1–10:18); central point of unit at 8:1–2. 10:19–39 closely associated with 11:1–40; Jesus in 12:1–3 climaxes history proper; broader sense 10:19–39 introduces entire concluding main section (judgment intimated by “coming one” 10:36–39 fruition at 12:25–29); outline puts major break between 10:39 and 11:1 as well as after 12:3. “You have come to Mount Zion” describes results of Christ’s session — hence Ps 110:1 parenthetical there.  
**Quote:** “Ps 110:4 (Heb 5:5-6; 5:10; 6:20; 7:1-25) gives 4:14-7:28 a certain coherence. … Thus, while recognizing the coherence that is there in 4:14-7:28 it is helpful when expounding this central section of Hebrews to divide it into four main parts … One must not forget, however, that the central point of the unit comes at 8:1-2. … The introductory material in 10:19-39 is closely associated with and flows into the history of the ancient faithful in 11: 1-40. … the outline at the end of this introduction has put a major break between 10:39 and 11:1 as well as at the pivotal point after 12:3. … \"You have come to Mount Zion\" describes the results of Christ's session. Thus we have here put Ps 110:1 in parentheses.”  
**Locus:** L1677–L1683
